paper.title: Admission to higher education programmes and student educational outcomes and earnings-Evidence from Denmark
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project number is given. …

registers.name_in_paper: the central admission system (data from the Ministry of Higher Education and Science)
registers.role: treatment, instrument and sample frame: the programmes listed in each application and their rankings, admission status for each student, and GPA thresholds for each programme (Quota 1 and standby)
variables_mentioned: programmes listed in each application and their rankings
GPA thresholds for each programme (Quota 1 and standby)

registers.name_in_paper: longitudinal administrative register data from Statistics Denmark
registers.years: applicants' GPAs from 1978 onwards; outcomes up to 11 (robustness: 16) years after the year of application, i.e. through about 2013
registers.role: outcomes, controls and linkage: applicants' GPAs from upper secondary school, yearly educational progression, earnings and demographics, and links from applicants to their parents and thereby parental education and earnings
variables_mentioned: yearly educational progression (Statistics Denmark programme codes: subject of study and level of education)

registers.name_in_paper: the population register (persons 'not in the population register at the end of this year' are treated as missing)
registers.role: linkage and attrition: identifies applicants who have emigrated or died, for whom outcomes 11 years after the YOA are missing (about 6%)

linkages: applications from the central admission system linked to Statistics Denmark register data using individuals' unique personal identification numbers
applicants linked to their parents, and thereby to parental education and earnings

a crosswalk established for each year of application from admission-system programme codes to Statistics Denmark programme codes, based on applicants admitted to their first-choice programmes who are enrolled in higher degree programmes in the YOA (recorded in October)

sample.universe: all student applications for post-secondary education in Denmark 1994-2002 handled by the central admission system (519,800 applications)
sample.unit_of_observation: applicant (one observation per individual, at her first application)
selection_rules: first application by the individual concerned (applicants who applied in 1993 are excluded entirely): 270,526
applicants were 25 years of age or younger in the year of application: 227,357
the first-choice programme is a higher degree programme: 83,046
a Quota 1 GPA threshold exists for the first-choice programme (restricted admission): 59,885
GPA is not missing, i.e. the applicant has a Danish upper secondary school qualification: 55,141 (Sample 1; DS10: 43,295)
a standby GPA threshold exists for any standby list of the first-choice programme: 52,724 (Sample 1s; DS10: 40,834)
a Quota 1 GPA threshold exists for all higher degree programmes listed in the application, which must also be ranked above other programme types: 46,485 (Sample 2; DS10: 36,746)
a standby GPA threshold exists for all higher degree programmes listed in the application: 43,624 (Sample 2s; DS10: 32,726)
also excluded: applicants who had already completed a post-secondary programme and applicants who had been enrolled in post-secondary education in previous years without completing it

estimation samples are further restricted to a discontinuity sample, DS10 (|GPA minus threshold| <= 1.0) or DS05 (<= 0.5), and in the main regressions applicants with GPA exactly equal to the threshold are dropped (donut design)
sample.period: application years 1994-2002; outcomes measured 11 years after the year of application
sample.n_observations: Sample 1: 55,141 (DS10 43,295); Sample 1s: 52,724 (DS10 40,834); Sample 2: 46,485 (DS10 36,746); Sample 2s: 43,624 (DS10 32,726). Main estimation samples (donut, DS10): 38,075 for admission outcomes and 35,814 for 11-year outcomes in Sample 1s; 30,634 and 28,844 in Sample 2s
sample.n_individuals: one observation per applicant, so the number of individuals equals the number of observations

construction_notes: the running variable is r_i = applicant's GPA from upper secondary school minus the relevant admission threshold; GPA is on the pre-2006 Danish scale with integer values 0-13 (omitting 1, 2, 4 and 12) and is calculated to one decimal place, so r is discrete with 5-10 values on each side of the threshold; its standard deviation in the full sample is 0.9
'standby threshold' means the standby threshold for programmes with a standby list and the Quota 1 threshold for programmes without one

in Samples 2 and 2s the relevant threshold is the lowest threshold among the higher degree programmes listed in the application, and the programme defining the programme-by-YOA fixed effects is the programme with that lowest threshold

'years of education' means the number of years needed to obtain the completed level of education: 12 years of primary and secondary school plus the prescribed period of study of the completed post-secondary programme (bachelor's = 15 years, master's = 17-18 years, nursing/teaching = 15.5-16 years)

completion of a master's degree in the preferred subject of study = a bachelor's degree in the preferred subject plus a master's degree in some subject within 11 years from the YOA; the field-of-study versions use the ISCED-F 2013 broad academic area of the preferred programme

outcome variables for enrolment and educational attainment use Statistics Denmark programme codes, which reflect subject of study and level but not institution, while the admission variables use detailed admission-system programme codes (subject and institution)
earnings are annual wage income; both parental income and applicants' earnings are deflated by the consumer price index with base year 2000
log earnings are restricted to individuals with earnings above the full-time full-year minimum wage (DKK 160,000, about USD 25,000, in year 2000)
parental income is the log of mean parental income in the YOA and the three preceding years; missing indicators are included for parental education and income
degree completion and earnings are measured 11 years after the YOA and are missing for about 6% of applicants due to emigration or death; enrolment is recorded in October of the YOA
currency conversions stated by the paper: USD 1 is about DKK 6.5 and EUR 1 about DKK 7.5 (2014-2016 average), i.e. DKK 1 is about USD 0.15

claims.statement: Crossing the standby admission threshold of the first-choice programme raises the probability of being admitted to the first-choice programme via Quota 1, Quota 2 or standby (the first stage of the fuzzy RD design).

treatment.label: Crossing the admission threshold: d = 1[r ≥ 0], where r is GPA minus the standby admission threshold of the first-choice programme (the standby threshold where the programme has a standby list, the Quota 1 threshold otherwise)

register_source.value: central admission system data from the Ministry of Higher Education and Science (GPA thresholds for each programme, Quota 1 and standby) combined with register information on applicants' GPAs from upper secondary school; no Statistics Denmark register code is named

definition.value: Dummy d_i equal to 1 if the applicant's GPA from upper secondary school is equal to or above the standby admission threshold of the first-choice programme (the standby threshold where the programme has a standby list, the Quota 1 threshold otherwise). The running variable r_i is the applicant's GPA minus that threshold; GPA is measured on the Danish 10-point scale and calculated to one decimal place.

timing.value: measured in the applicant's first year of application (YOA), 1994-2002; thresholds are published at the end of July, after all applications have been submitted

register_source.value: central admission system data from the Ministry of Higher Education and Science (admission status, programmes listed and their ranking, Quota 1 and standby GPA thresholds); no Statistics Denmark register code is named

definition.value: Dummy = 1 if the applicant is admitted to the first-choice programme via Quota 1, Quota 2 or the standby list in the first year of application

timing.value: year of application (YOA)

units.value: share (0-1 dummy outcome); a coefficient of 0.100 corresponds to 10.0 percentage points

magnitude.interpretation: The discontinuity in admission probability is between 64 and 73 percentage points according to the point estimates in Table 5; 0.728 in the main specification.

estimand.target_population: marginal applicants, i.e. applicants with a GPA close to the standby threshold of their first-choice programme
estimand.time_horizon: admission in the applicant's first year of application
estimand.formal_query: E[admitted_1st_choice_pgme_q1_q2_standby | do(d = 1)] - E[admitted_1st_choice_pgme_q1_q2_standby | do(d = 0)] for applicants at the standby admission threshold of their first-choice programme (an intention to treat effect of meeting the GPA qualification)

population.description: Sample 1s: first-time applicants to Danish post-secondary education 1994-2002 who were 25 years of age or younger in the year of application, had not previously completed or been enrolled in post-secondary education, had a non-missing GPA from Danish upper secondary school, and whose first-choice programme was a higher degree (university) programme with a restricted-admission Quota 1 GPA threshold and a restricted standby threshold; restricted here to the DS10 discontinuity sample (|r| <= 1.0) with applicants whose GPA exactly equals the threshold excluded (donut)
population.ages: 25 years of age or younger in the year of application (mean age 20.8)
population.period: application years 1994-2002
subgroups_defined: preferred broad academic area (arts and humanities; social science; law; natural science; architecture and engineering; veterinary and forestry; medicine and dentistry)
specific preferred subject of study (results shown for medicine and law)
population.selection: applicants are selected on having applied for the first time in 1994-2002, on age <= 25, on not having completed or been enrolled in post-secondary education before, on having a Danish upper secondary school GPA, and on their first-choice programme having both a Quota 1 and a standby admission threshold; the estimation sample is further restricted to |r| <= 1.0 with r = 0 excluded, and outcome samples are censored on being in the registers 11 years after the YOA

identification.source_of_variation: Discontinuity at the standby GPA admission threshold of the first-choice programme: all applicants with a GPA above the published threshold are admitted, the threshold varies across programmes and across application years 1994-2002, and it is published only after all applications have been submitted

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable and no anticipation of the threshold: applicants cannot exactly control their GPA and the admission threshold is published only after all applications have been submitted and student places allocated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Histograms of the running variable (Fig. 1) show no discontinuity at the threshold, and the Cattaneo, Jansson and Ma (2017a,b) density test (applicable to a discrete running variable) does not reject smoothness at 0.0 or 0.1 in any of the four samples (p-values 0.14-0.98, Appendix Table A.2); the average within-programme standard deviation of the threshold over 1994-2002 is 0.18 (Quota 1) and 0.24 (standby) grade points.

key_assumptions.assumption: Local randomization: applicants with GPAs just above and just below the threshold have very similar observable and unobservable characteristics affecting outcomes, so that conditional on the running variable and programme-by-YOA fixed effects, threshold crossing is independent of the unobserved determinants of the outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Covariate balance tests at the threshold for every control variable (Appendix Table A.3; only 8 of 88 jumps significant at 5%, 5 of them for age, and none significant with a second-order polynomial, Table A.4), jump tests on predicted outcomes (all p-values above 0.11), and the density tests; the paper concludes the evidence supports local randomization.

key_assumptions.assumption: Regression-based extrapolation to the threshold is valid: because the running variable is discrete (5-10 values on each side of the threshold), the expected outcome at the threshold must be obtained by extrapolating the fitted polynomial from each side.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper shows results for alternative bandwidths (DS10, DS05 and every bandwidth from 0.1 to 1.5), for first- and second-order polynomials, and for a triangular instead of a uniform kernel.

threats_discussed: psychological effects of having a GPA just below rather than just above the threshold, given admission status, would violate the exclusion restriction
no information on who applies for the standby list or for Quota 2, so the paper cannot check that the shares applying are the same on each side of the thresholds

the running variable is discrete and coarse (5-10 values on each side of the threshold), so optimal-bandwidth methods assuming a continuous running variable do not apply and regression-based extrapolation to the threshold is required
only some applicants with a GPA exactly equal to the threshold are admitted (age precedence or random selection), which motivates the donut design
clustered standard errors with few clusters on the running variable may be biased (Kolesar & Rothe, 2016)
the relation between admission and the running variable is non-linear just above the threshold because some applicants do not apply for standby admission
educational attainment and earnings 11 years after the YOA are missing for about 6% of applicants (emigration or death), so the estimation sample is censored on the outcome
robustness_checks: narrower bandwidth DS05 (|r| <= 0.5) alongside DS10 (|r| <= 1.0) -- columns (5)-(7)
second-order polynomial in the running variable on each side of the threshold -- column (3)
'Incl. 0' design retaining applicants with GPA exactly equal to the threshold for programmes where all such applicants are admitted -- columns (4) and (7)
estimates and confidence intervals for every bandwidth from 0.1 to 1.5 (Appendix figures)
four alternative sets of clustered standard errors (running variable; running variable x YOA; programme; programme x YOA) reported in the Appendix
triangular instead of uniform kernel
outcomes measured 10 years and up to 16 years after the YOA
alternative earnings measure including earnings from self-employment
alternative lower thresholds for log earnings (DKK 100,000 or 200,000) and trimming the top 1% or 5% of the earnings distribution
restricting the sample to applicants from 1999-2002 (GPA coverage)
sample extended to applicants whose first choice is a 2-4 year professionally oriented programme
subgroup estimations by preferred broad academic area and by specific subject of study
unresolved_confounders: whether the shares of applicants applying for standby and/or Quota 2 admission are the same on each side of the thresholds cannot be checked, because the data do not record who applied for those channels
the excludability assumption (notably psychological effects of threshold crossing given admission status) cannot be tested

estimator.value: OLS reduced form RD regression of the outcome on the threshold-crossing dummy d, with a first-order polynomial in the running variable estimated separately on each side of the threshold

estimation.specification: Eq. (2): yi = α + βdi + δ1 ri + δ2 ri di + ui, estimated on Sample 1s in the DS10 discontinuity sample (|r| <= 1.0) with r = 0 excluded (donut), with programme-by-YOA fixed effects and controls for age, age squared, gender, immigrant status and parental education and income; uniform kernel; standard errors clustered on programme (Table 5, column (2))
fixed_effects: programme-by-YOA fixed effects (programme = the first-choice programme in Samples 1 and 1s, the programme with the lowest admission threshold among the listed programmes in Samples 2 and 2s)
controls: first-order polynomial in the running variable r, estimated separately on each side of the threshold (r and r x d)
log mother's income (mean parental income in the YOA and the three preceding years, CPI-deflated)
log father's income (mean parental income in the YOA and the three preceding years, CPI-deflated)
estimation.clustering: robust standard errors clustered on education programme applied for (the most conservative of four clustering choices examined)
estimation.weights: uniform kernel within the bandwidth (no observation weights)

source_table.value: Table 5, column (2) (DS10, donut, first-order polynomial, with demographic and parental controls)

adjustment_set.label: running variable r = GPA minus the relevant admission threshold, with separate slopes on each side of the threshold
programme-by-YOA fixed effects
age at application and age squared
gender
immigrant status
parental education (mother's and father's years of education, with missing indicators)
parental income (log mean income of mother and father in the YOA and the three preceding years, with missing indicators)

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable and no anticipation of the threshold: applicants cannot exactly control their GPA and the admission threshold is published only after all applications have been submitted and student places allocated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Histograms of the running variable (Fig. 1) show no discontinuity at the threshold, and the Cattaneo, Jansson and Ma (2017a,b) density test (applicable to a discrete running variable) does not reject smoothness at 0.0 or 0.1 in any of the four samples (p-values 0.14-0.98, Appendix Table A.2); the average within-programme standard deviation of the threshold over 1994-2002 is 0.18 (Quota 1) and 0.24 (standby) grade points.

key_assumptions.assumption: Local randomization: applicants with GPAs just above and just below the threshold have very similar observable and unobservable characteristics affecting outcomes, so that conditional on the running variable and programme-by-YOA fixed effects, threshold crossing is independent of the unobserved determinants of the outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Covariate balance tests at the threshold for every control variable (Appendix Table A.3; only 8 of 88 jumps significant at 5%, 5 of them for age, and none significant with a second-order polynomial, Table A.4), jump tests on predicted outcomes (all p-values above 0.11), and the density tests; the paper concludes the evidence supports local randomization.

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable and no anticipation of the threshold: applicants cannot exactly control their GPA and the admission threshold is published only after all applications have been submitted and student places allocated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Histograms of the running variable (Fig. 1) show no discontinuity at the threshold, and the Cattaneo, Jansson and Ma (2017a,b) density test (applicable to a discrete running variable) does not reject smoothness at 0.0 or 0.1 in any of the four samples (p-values 0.14-0.98, Appendix Table A.2); the average within-programme standard deviation of the threshold over 1994-2002 is 0.18 (Quota 1) and 0.24 (standby) grade points.

key_assumptions.assumption: Local randomization: applicants with GPAs just above and just below the threshold have very similar observable and unobservable characteristics affecting outcomes, so that conditional on the running variable and programme-by-YOA fixed effects, threshold crossing is independent of the unobserved determinants of the outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Covariate balance tests at the threshold for every control variable (Appendix Table A.3; only 8 of 88 jumps significant at 5%, 5 of them for age, and none significant with a second-order polynomial, Table A.4), jump tests on predicted outcomes (all p-values above 0.11), and the density tests; the paper concludes the evidence supports local randomization.

key_assumptions.assumption: Excludability: crossing the admission threshold affects outcomes only through its effect on the likelihood of admission to a preferred programme in the YOA.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the assumption seems very likely to hold but cannot be tested, names psychological effects of being just below rather than just above the threshold as the threat, and reports reduced form estimates which are unbiased even if excludability fails.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance (a strong first stage): threshold crossing raises the probability of admission discontinuously at the threshold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: F test statistics for the instrument in the first-stage regressions are reported at the bottom of Table 6: 907 for the degree/earnings sample and 763 for the log earnings sample in column (2).

key_assumptions.assumption: Monotonicity: a GPA just above the threshold (as opposed to just below) does not reduce the probability of admission for any student.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states this is clearly the case, and characterises compliers, always-takers and never-takers in terms of Quota 2 and programme-specific admission criteria.

key_assumptions.assumption: Regression-based extrapolation to the threshold is valid: because the running variable is discrete (5-10 values on each side of the threshold), the expected outcome at the threshold must be obtained by extrapolating the fitted polynomial from each side.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper shows results for alternative bandwidths (DS10, DS05 and every bandwidth from 0.1 to 1.5), for first- and second-order polynomials, and for a triangular instead of a uniform kernel.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential selection out of the estimation sample: outcomes 11 years after the YOA are missing for about 6% of applicants (emigration or death), so the estimation sample is conditioned on non-missing outcome data; threshold crossing must not affect the probability that these data are missing.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Jump tests for the missing-data dummy at the threshold (Appendix Fig. A.5 and the last row of Appendix Table A.3) show no evidence of an effect on missingness.

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable and no anticipation of the threshold: applicants cannot exactly control their GPA and the admission threshold is published only after all applications have been submitted and student places allocated.

key_assumptions.assumption: Local randomization: applicants with GPAs just above and just below the threshold have very similar observable and unobservable characteristics affecting outcomes, so that conditional on the running variable and programme-by-YOA fixed effects, threshold crossing is independent of the unobserved determinants of the outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Covariate balance tests at the threshold for every control variable (Appendix Table A.3; only 8 of 88 jumps significant at 5%, 5 of them for age, and none significant with a second-order polynomial, Table A.4), jump tests on predicted outcomes (all p-values above 0.11), and the density tests; the paper concludes the evidence supports local randomization.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance (a strong first stage): threshold crossing raises the probability of admission discontinuously at the threshold.

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable and no anticipation of the threshold: applicants cannot exactly control their GPA and the admission threshold is published only after all applications have been submitted and student places allocated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Histograms of the running variable (Fig. 1) show no discontinuity at the threshold, and the Cattaneo, Jansson and Ma (2017a,b) density test (applicable to a discrete running variable) does not reject smoothness at 0.0 or 0.1 in any of the four samples (p-values 0.14-0.98, Appendix Table A.2); the average within-programme standard deviation of the threshold over 1994-2002 is 0.18 (Quota 1) and 0.24 (standby) grade points.

key_assumptions.assumption: Local randomization: applicants with GPAs just above and just below the threshold have very similar observable and unobservable characteristics affecting outcomes, so that conditional on the running variable and programme-by-YOA fixed effects, threshold crossing is independent of the unobserved determinants of the outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Covariate balance tests at the threshold for every control variable (Appendix Table A.3; only 8 of 88 jumps significant at 5%, 5 of them for age, and none significant with a second-order polynomial, Table A.4), jump tests on predicted outcomes (all p-values above 0.11), and the density tests; the paper concludes the evidence supports local randomization.

key_assumptions.assumption: Regression-based extrapolation to the threshold is valid: because the running variable is discrete (5-10 values on each side of the threshold), the expected outcome at the threshold must be obtained by extrapolating the fitted polynomial from each side.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper shows results for alternative bandwidths (DS10, DS05 and every bandwidth from 0.1 to 1.5), for first- and second-order polynomials, and for a triangular instead of a uniform kernel.

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable and no anticipation of the threshold: applicants cannot exactly control their GPA and the admission threshold is published only after all applications have been submitted and student places allocated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Histograms of the running variable (Fig. 1) show no discontinuity at the threshold, and the Cattaneo, Jansson and Ma (2017a,b) density test (applicable to a discrete running variable) does not reject smoothness at 0.0 or 0.1 in any of the four samples (p-values 0.14-0.98, Appendix Table A.2); the average within-programme standard deviation of the threshold over 1994-2002 is 0.18 (Quota 1) and 0.24 (standby) grade points.

key_assumptions.assumption: Local randomization: applicants with GPAs just above and just below the threshold have very similar observable and unobservable characteristics affecting outcomes, so that conditional on the running variable and programme-by-YOA fixed effects, threshold crossing is independent of the unobserved determinants of the outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Covariate balance tests at the threshold for every control variable (Appendix Table A.3; only 8 of 88 jumps significant at 5%, 5 of them for age, and none significant with a second-order polynomial, Table A.4), jump tests on predicted outcomes (all p-values above 0.11), and the density tests; the paper concludes the evidence supports local randomization.

key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper shows results for alternative bandwidths (DS10, DS05 and every bandwidth from 0.1 to 1.5), for first- and second-order polynomials, and for a triangular instead of a uniform kernel.

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable and no anticipation of the threshold: applicants cannot exactly control their GPA and the admission threshold is published only after all applications have been submitted and student places allocated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Histograms of the running variable (Fig. 1) show no discontinuity at the threshold, and the Cattaneo, Jansson and Ma (2017a,b) density test (applicable to a discrete running variable) does not reject smoothness at 0.0 or 0.1 in any of the four samples (p-values 0.14-0.98, Appendix Table A.2); the average within-programme standard deviation of the threshold over 1994-2002 is 0.18 (Quota 1) and 0.24 (standby) grade points.

key_assumptions.assumption: Local randomization: applicants with GPAs just above and just below the threshold have very similar observable and unobservable characteristics affecting outcomes, so that conditional on the running variable and programme-by-YOA fixed effects, threshold crossing is independent of the unobserved determinants of the outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Covariate balance tests at the threshold for every control variable (Appendix Table A.3; only 8 of 88 jumps significant at 5%, 5 of them for age, and none significant with a second-order polynomial, Table A.4), jump tests on predicted outcomes (all p-values above 0.11), and the density tests; the paper concludes the evidence supports local randomization.

key_assumptions.assumption: Excludability: crossing the admission threshold affects outcomes only through its effect on the likelihood of admission to a preferred programme in the YOA.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the assumption seems very likely to hold but cannot be tested, names psychological effects of being just below rather than just above the threshold as the threat, and reports reduced form estimates which are unbiased even if excludability fails.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance (a strong first stage): threshold crossing raises the probability of admission discontinuously at the threshold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: F test statistics for the instrument in the first-stage regressions are reported at the bottom of Table 8: 899 for the degree/earnings sample and 801 for the log earnings sample in column (2).

key_assumptions.assumption: Monotonicity: a GPA just above the threshold (as opposed to just below) does not reduce the probability of admission for any student.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states this is clearly the case, and characterises compliers, always-takers and never-takers in terms of Quota 2 and programme-specific admission criteria.

key_assumptions.assumption: Regression-based extrapolation to the threshold is valid: because the running variable is discrete (5-10 values on each side of the threshold), the expected outcome at the threshold must be obtained by extrapolating the fitted polynomial from each side.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper shows results for alternative bandwidths (DS10, DS05 and every bandwidth from 0.1 to 1.5), for first- and second-order polynomials, and for a triangular instead of a uniform kernel.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential selection out of the estimation sample: outcomes 11 years after the YOA are missing for about 6% of applicants (emigration or death), so the estimation sample is conditioned on non-missing outcome data; threshold crossing must not affect the probability that these data are missing.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Jump tests for the missing-data dummy at the threshold (Appendix Fig. A.5 and the last row of Appendix Table A.3) show no evidence of an effect on missingness.

identification.source_of_variation: Discontinuity at the Quota 1 GPA admission threshold of the first-choice programme (direct admission via Quotas 1 or 2)

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable and no anticipation of the threshold: applicants cannot exactly control their GPA and the admission threshold is published only after all applications have been submitted and student places allocated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Histograms of the running variable (Fig. 1) show no discontinuity at the threshold, and the Cattaneo, Jansson and Ma (2017a,b) density test (applicable to a discrete running variable) does not reject smoothness at 0.0 or 0.1 in any of the four samples (p-values 0.14-0.98, Appendix Table A.2); the average within-programme standard deviation of the threshold over 1994-2002 is 0.18 (Quota 1) and 0.24 (standby) grade points.

key_assumptions.assumption: Local randomization: applicants with GPAs just above and just below the threshold have very similar observable and unobservable characteristics affecting outcomes, so that conditional on the running variable and programme-by-YOA fixed effects, threshold crossing is independent of the unobserved determinants of the outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Covariate balance tests at the threshold for every control variable (Appendix Table A.3; only 8 of 88 jumps significant at 5%, 5 of them for age, and none significant with a second-order polynomial, Table A.4), jump tests on predicted outcomes (all p-values above 0.11), and the density tests; the paper concludes the evidence supports local randomization.

key_assumptions.assumption: Regression-based extrapolation to the threshold is valid: because the running variable is discrete (5-10 values on each side of the threshold), the expected outcome at the threshold must be obtained by extrapolating the fitted polynomial from each side.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper shows results for alternative bandwidths (DS10, DS05 and every bandwidth from 0.1 to 1.5), for first- and second-order polynomials, and for a triangular instead of a uniform kernel.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential selection out of the estimation sample: outcomes 11 years after the YOA are missing for about 6% of applicants (emigration or death), so the estimation sample is conditioned on non-missing outcome data; threshold crossing must not affect the probability that these data are missing.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Jump tests for the missing-data dummy at the threshold (Appendix Fig. A.5 and the last row of Appendix Table A.3) show no evidence of an effect on missingness.

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable and no anticipation of the threshold: applicants cannot exactly control their GPA and the admission threshold is published only after all applications have been submitted and student places allocated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Histograms of the running variable (Fig. 1) show no discontinuity at the threshold, and the Cattaneo, Jansson and Ma (2017a,b) density test (applicable to a discrete running variable) does not reject smoothness at 0.0 or 0.1 in any of the four samples (p-values 0.14-0.98, Appendix Table A.2); the average within-programme standard deviation of the threshold over 1994-2002 is 0.18 (Quota 1) and 0.24 (standby) grade points.

key_assumptions.assumption: Local randomization: applicants with GPAs just above and just below the threshold have very similar observable and unobservable characteristics affecting outcomes, so that conditional on the running variable and programme-by-YOA fixed effects, threshold crossing is independent of the unobserved determinants of the outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Covariate balance tests at the threshold for every control variable (Appendix Table A.3; only 8 of 88 jumps significant at 5%, 5 of them for age, and none significant with a second-order polynomial, Table A.4), jump tests on predicted outcomes (all p-values above 0.11), and the density tests; the paper concludes the evidence supports local randomization.

key_assumptions.assumption: Excludability: crossing the admission threshold affects outcomes only through its effect on the likelihood of admission to a preferred programme in the YOA.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states the assumption seems very likely to hold but cannot be tested, names psychological effects of being just below rather than just above the threshold as the threat, and reports reduced form estimates which are unbiased even if excludability fails.

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance (a strong first stage): threshold crossing raises the probability of admission discontinuously at the threshold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The share admitted is constant and close to 1 above the threshold and the discontinuity in admission is 0.78-0.79, not affected by choice of bandwidth (p. 15).

key_assumptions.assumption: Monotonicity: a GPA just above the threshold (as opposed to just below) does not reduce the probability of admission for any student.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper states this is clearly the case, and characterises compliers, always-takers and never-takers in terms of Quota 2 and programme-specific admission criteria.

key_assumptions.assumption: Regression-based extrapolation to the threshold is valid: because the running variable is discrete (5-10 values on each side of the threshold), the expected outcome at the threshold must be obtained by extrapolating the fitted polynomial from each side.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper shows results for alternative bandwidths (DS10, DS05 and every bandwidth from 0.1 to 1.5), for first- and second-order polynomials, and for a triangular instead of a uniform kernel.

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable and no anticipation of the threshold: applicants cannot exactly control their GPA and the admission threshold is published only after all applications have been submitted and student places allocated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Histograms of the running variable (Fig. 1) show no discontinuity at the threshold, and the Cattaneo, Jansson and Ma (2017a,b) density test (applicable to a discrete running variable) does not reject smoothness at 0.0 or 0.1 in any of the four samples (p-values 0.14-0.98, Appendix Table A.2); the average within-programme standard deviation of the threshold over 1994-2002 is 0.18 (Quota 1) and 0.24 (standby) grade points.

key_assumptions.assumption: Local randomization: applicants with GPAs just above and just below the threshold have very similar observable and unobservable characteristics affecting outcomes, so that conditional on the running variable and programme-by-YOA fixed effects, threshold crossing is independent of the unobserved determinants of the outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Covariate balance tests at the threshold for every control variable (Appendix Table A.3; only 8 of 88 jumps significant at 5%, 5 of them for age, and none significant with a second-order polynomial, Table A.4), jump tests on predicted outcomes (all p-values above 0.11), and the density tests; the paper concludes the evidence supports local randomization.

population.description: Sample 1: first-time applicants 1994-2002, aged 25 or younger in the YOA, no prior post-secondary education, non-missing GPA, first-choice programme a higher degree programme with a Quota 1 GPA threshold; the threshold is the Quota 1 threshold of the first-choice programme and admission is admission via Quotas 1 or 2
population.ages: 25 years of age or younger in the year of application

specific preferred subject of study (results shown for medicine and law)

identification.source_of_variation: Discontinuity at the Quota 1 GPA admission threshold of the first-choice programme (direct admission via Quotas 1 or 2)

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable and no anticipation of the threshold: applicants cannot exactly control their GPA and the admission threshold is published only after all applications have been submitted and student places allocated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Histograms of the running variable (Fig. 1) show no discontinuity at the threshold, and the Cattaneo, Jansson and Ma (2017a,b) density test (applicable to a discrete running variable) does not reject smoothness at 0.0 or 0.1 in any of the four samples (p-values 0.14-0.98, Appendix Table A.2); the average within-programme standard deviation of the threshold over 1994-2002 is 0.18 (Quota 1) and 0.24 (standby) grade points.

key_assumptions.assumption: Local randomization: applicants with GPAs just above and just below the threshold have very similar observable and unobservable characteristics affecting outcomes, so that conditional on the running variable and programme-by-YOA fixed effects, threshold crossing is independent of the unobserved determinants of the outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Covariate balance tests at the threshold for every control variable (Appendix Table A.3; only 8 of 88 jumps significant at 5%, 5 of them for age, and none significant with a second-order polynomial, Table A.4), jump tests on predicted outcomes (all p-values above 0.11), and the density tests; the paper concludes the evidence supports local randomization.

key_assumptions.assumption: Regression-based extrapolation to the threshold is valid: because the running variable is discrete (5-10 values on each side of the threshold), the expected outcome at the threshold must be obtained by extrapolating the fitted polynomial from each side.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper shows results for alternative bandwidths (DS10, DS05 and every bandwidth from 0.1 to 1.5), for first- and second-order polynomials, and for a triangular instead of a uniform kernel.

threats_discussed: psychological effects of having a GPA just below rather than just above the threshold, given admission status, would violate the exclusion restriction
no information on who applies for the standby list or for Quota 2, so the paper cannot check that the shares applying are the same on each side of the thresholds

the running variable is discrete and coarse (5-10 values on each side of the threshold), so optimal-bandwidth methods assuming a continuous running variable do not apply and regression-based extrapolation to the threshold is required
only some applicants with a GPA exactly equal to the threshold are admitted (age precedence or random selection), which motivates the donut design
clustered standard errors with few clusters on the running variable may be biased (Kolesar & Rothe, 2016)
the relation between admission and the running variable is non-linear just above the threshold because some applicants do not apply for standby admission
educational attainment and earnings 11 years after the YOA are missing for about 6% of applicants (emigration or death), so the estimation sample is censored on the outcome
robustness_checks: narrower bandwidth DS05 (|r| <= 0.5) alongside DS10 (|r| <= 1.0) -- columns (5)-(7)
second-order polynomial in the running variable on each side of the threshold -- column (3)
'Incl. 0' design retaining applicants with GPA exactly equal to the threshold for programmes where all such applicants are admitted -- columns (4) and (7)
estimates and confidence intervals for every bandwidth from 0.1 to 1.5 (Appendix figures)
four alternative sets of clustered standard errors (running variable; running variable x YOA; programme; programme x YOA) reported in the Appendix
triangular instead of uniform kernel
outcomes measured 10 years and up to 16 years after the YOA
alternative earnings measure including earnings from self-employment
alternative lower thresholds for log earnings (DKK 100,000 or 200,000) and trimming the top 1% or 5% of the earnings distribution
restricting the sample to applicants from 1999-2002 (GPA coverage)
sample extended to applicants whose first choice is a 2-4 year professionally oriented programme
subgroup estimations by preferred broad academic area and by specific subject of study
unresolved_confounders: whether the shares of applicants applying for standby and/or Quota 2 admission are the same on each side of the thresholds cannot be checked, because the data do not record who applied for those channels
the excludability assumption (notably psychological effects of threshold crossing given admission status) cannot be tested

key_assumptions.assumption: No manipulation of the running variable and no anticipation of the threshold: applicants cannot exactly control their GPA and the admission threshold is published only after all applications have been submitted and student places allocated.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Histograms of the running variable (Fig. 1) show no discontinuity at the threshold, and the Cattaneo, Jansson and Ma (2017a,b) density test (applicable to a discrete running variable) does not reject smoothness at 0.0 or 0.1 in any of the four samples (p-values 0.14-0.98, Appendix Table A.2); the average within-programme standard deviation of the threshold over 1994-2002 is 0.18 (Quota 1) and 0.24 (standby) grade points.

key_assumptions.assumption: Local randomization: applicants with GPAs just above and just below the threshold have very similar observable and unobservable characteristics affecting outcomes, so that conditional on the running variable and programme-by-YOA fixed effects, threshold crossing is independent of the unobserved determinants of the outcome.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Covariate balance tests at the threshold for every control variable (Appendix Table A.3; only 8 of 88 jumps significant at 5%, 5 of them for age, and none significant with a second-order polynomial, Table A.4), jump tests on predicted outcomes (all p-values above 0.11), and the density tests; the paper concludes the evidence supports local randomization.

key_assumptions.assumption: Regression-based extrapolation to the threshold is valid: because the running variable is discrete (5-10 values on each side of the threshold), the expected outcome at the threshold must be obtained by extrapolating the fitted polynomial from each side.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper shows results for alternative bandwidths (DS10, DS05 and every bandwidth from 0.1 to 1.5), for first- and second-order polynomials, and for a triangular instead of a uniform kernel.

key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper shows results for alternative bandwidths (DS10, DS05 and every bandwidth from 0.1 to 1.5), for first- and second-order polynomials, and for a triangular instead of a uniform kernel.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential selection out of the estimation sample: outcomes 11 years after the YOA are missing for about 6% of applicants (emigration or death), so the estimation sample is conditioned on non-missing outcome data; threshold crossing must not affect the probability that these data are missing.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Jump tests for the missing-data dummy at the threshold (Appendix Fig. A.5 and the last row of Appendix Table A.3) show no evidence of an effect on missingness.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Covariate balance tests at the threshold for every control variable (Appendix Table A.3; only 8 of 88 jumps significant at 5%, 5 of them for age, and none significant with a second-order polynomial, Table A.4), jump tests on predicted outcomes (all p-values above 0.11), and the density tests; the paper concludes the evidence supports local randomization.

key_assumptions.assumption: Regression-based extrapolation to the threshold is valid: because the running variable is discrete (5-10 values on each side of the threshold), the expected outcome at the threshold must be obtained by extrapolating the fitted polynomial from each side.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper shows results for alternative bandwidths (DS10, DS05 and every bandwidth from 0.1 to 1.5), for first- and second-order polynomials, and for a triangular instead of a uniform kernel.

key_assumptions.assumption: No differential selection out of the estimation sample: outcomes 11 years after the YOA are missing for about 6% of applicants (emigration or death), so the estimation sample is conditioned on non-missing outcome data; threshold crossing must not affect the probability that these data are missing.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Jump tests for the missing-data dummy at the threshold (Appendix Fig. A.5 and the last row of Appendix Table A.3) show no evidence of an effect on missingness.

threats_discussed: psychological effects of having a GPA just below rather than just above the threshold, given admission status, would violate the exclusion restriction
no information on who applies for the standby list or for Quota 2, so the paper cannot check that the shares applying are the same on each side of the thresholds

the running variable is discrete and coarse (5-10 values on each side of the threshold), so optimal-bandwidth methods assuming a continuous running variable do not apply and regression-based extrapolation to the threshold is required
only some applicants with a GPA exactly equal to the threshold are admitted (age precedence or random selection), which motivates the donut design
clustered standard errors with few clusters on the running variable may be biased (Kolesar & Rothe, 2016)
the relation between admission and the running variable is non-linear just above the threshold because some applicants do not apply for standby admission
educational attainment and earnings 11 years after the YOA are missing for about 6% of applicants (emigration or death), so the estimation sample is censored on the outcome
